title: High-yield perennial versions of the major grain-crop portfolio

concept.text: The innovation is a portfolio of major grain crops that regrow after harvest and produce competitive, stable grain harvests for several years from one planting. The target combines persistence with agricultural productivity: plants must survive between harvests, regrow successfully, remain fertile and repeatedly produce useful grain yields. Success would include workable management and farm economics across representative production environments, rather than perennial growth alone.

Perennial rice supplies a demonstrated component of this vision. The broader concept concerns extending comparable capabilities across a major cereal portfolio, including crops with different biology and growing conditions. As a scope choice, the innovation does not require a single master regulatory module or one transferable genetic solution: different crops could reach the target through different breeding and management approaches.

significance.text: If achieved across major cereals and representative environments, productive perennial regrowth could change the recurring establishment cycle underlying much of grain agriculture. Where regrowth replaces replanting, farmers could avoid repeated establishment operations and their associated labour and disturbance. The rice study provides a concrete precedent: regrowth crops did not require a new seedling nursery, ploughing or transplanting to initiate each harvest cycle. Extending that mechanism across cereals could substantially change field operations, although widespread deployment is not demonstrated by the supplied evidence.

Environmental gains are conditional consequences to measure, rather than automatic properties of perennial grain production. Reduced disturbance and persistent roots could contribute to improved soil condition, but greater soil-water capacity does not establish lower water consumption. Likewise, soil-carbon accumulation alone does not establish lower lifecycle greenhouse-gas emissions. In flooded rice, potentially opposing methane and nitrous oxide effects make the full emissions balance especially important. Net benefits also depend on yields, inputs, pest and weed management, and how often stands need replacement.

Synthesis: The revolutionary potential lies in changing a widespread production cycle while retaining the grain output and economic performance farmers need. It does not imply universal suitability, indefinite stand life or guaranteed adoption. No historical calibration examples were supplied, so a precise comparison with past agricultural breakthroughs would go beyond this record.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central technical challenge is to combine durable survival and regrowth with repeated, competitive grain production across crops and environments. Persistence by itself is insufficient: each successive crop must also achieve adequate fertility and grain yield. Breeding and agronomy must make these traits work together over multiple seasons, rather than demonstrate a productive initial harvest followed by weak or unreliable regrowth.

Concrete barriers include survival under unsuitable temperatures, maintaining subsequent harvest yields, and controlling weeds and pests in a persistent stand. These are practical constraints as well as biological ones: a crop that regrows but requires costly management or frequent stand replacement may not deliver the intended advantage. The rice evidence includes pest damage and declining later yields, showing why multi-year durability and management must be evaluated together.

Evidence boundary: The supplied material establishes the research challenge and a successful irrigated-rice component; it does not establish whether the full cross-crop capability remains absent as of 1 November 2026. The supplied freshness-search record is empty. Accordingly, the broader portfolio is unestablished in this record, rather than proven unavailable today.

current_state.text: Zhang and colleagues’ study, “Sustained productivity and agronomic potential of perennial rice,” was published online in Nature Sustainability on 7 November 2022, despite its January 2023 volume date. It reported eight consecutive grain harvests over four years from one planting of irrigated perennial rice. Mean yields were 6.8 Mg ha−1 harvest−1 for perennial rice and 6.7 Mg ha−1 harvest−1 for the replanted annual-rice comparator. These are average yields per harvest, not annual totals or a guarantee of equivalent performance at every site.

The reviewed methods describe adjacent farmer-managed plots at three locations in Yunnan. The result therefore demonstrates substantial repeated production within a particular irrigated production setting, rather than globally representative cereal performance. Xinping experienced pest damage and lower subsequent yields, and yields declined in year five. The four-year result supports productive persistence over that interval; it does not establish indefinite productivity or uniformly stable performance under all local conditions.

The article documents a broader effort to develop perennial counterparts of annual crops, including wheat, barley, sorghum and rice. That development effort is distinct from demonstrating a competitive portfolio across their growing regions. The supplied rice result cannot establish equivalent achievements in wheat, maize or other major cereals, nor does it establish performance across all rice environments. Developments after this dated study remain unassessed in the supplied record; that limitation does not invalidate the rice demonstration.

The supplied review verified the article’s identity and assessed substantive extracted prose, including the abstract, results and methods. Its inspection was partial: some PDF pages lacked readable extracted content, figure images were not inspected, and supplementary tables were not supplied. The harvest counts and yield averages above were explicitly reported in readable prose, but this record does not provide an independent inspection of every graphical or supplementary detail. These access limitations constrain verification rather than demonstrate that the reported findings are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: Establish perennial versions of multiple major cereals in representative production environments and compare repeated harvests with well-managed annual systems over multiple years. Measure cumulative grain production over a common time interval, survival, regrowth, fertility, yield stability and stand-replacement frequency. The protocol should identify the crop set, duration, environments and competitiveness thresholds in advance. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Multiple perennial cereals meet predefined multiyear grain competitiveness thresholds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical test: Demonstrate competitive farmer economics after accounting for establishment savings, ongoing inputs, weed and pest control, harvest operations and eventual stand replacement. Record adverse seasons and management failures as well as successful harvests. The rice study’s assessment of productivity, livelihoods and management risks provides a precedent for this combined evaluation, but does not prescribe a complete portfolio-wide protocol.
completion_criteria.label: Competitive farmer economics include full production and replacement costs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed environmental test: Compare soil condition, soil-carbon changes, water use, pests and lifecycle greenhouse-gas emissions with suitable annual comparators. Specify environmental sampling and lifecycle boundaries, and include methane and nitrous oxide where relevant. Report water-holding capacity separately from actual water consumption, and soil-carbon gains separately from net emissions, so that one favourable measurement does not stand in for the complete environmental balance.
completion_criteria.label: Complete environmental balances are reported against suitable annual comparators

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and scope test: Seek independent replication across sites, seasons and farming teams using documented plant material, management and accessible results. Publish the climatic and management boundaries within which performance holds, including where stands fail or lose competitiveness. Finite trials can establish demonstrated breadth and reliability within tested conditions; they cannot establish literal universality across crops or environments.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication documents performance boundaries across tested farming conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — AGR-01, “Cereal crops supplied predominantly by biological nitrogen fixation,” concerns the source of crop nitrogen, while AGR-04 concerns persistence and repeated grain harvests. The capabilities could coexist, but perennial regrowth does not demonstrate adequate biological nitrogen supply. AGR-02, “A transferable carbon-concentrating system for C3 staple crops,” targets photosynthetic performance; improved carbon capture could complement grain productivity, but does not by itself establish survival, regrowth or multi-year fertility.

Roster-based synthesis — AGR-03, “Reliable clonal seed reproduction across major hybrid crops,” concerns preserving crop genotypes through seed reproduction. AGR-04 concerns continued production from an established stand. These address different routes to continuity: reliable clonal seed would not itself make a crop perennial. AGR-07, “A general, rapid method for creating productive crops from wild plants,” could offer a route to developing perennial grain crops from suitable wild material, but a general domestication method and a productive perennial cereal portfolio remain separate achievements.

Roster-based synthesis — AGR-05, “Productive staple farming with seawater and a closed salt balance,” concerns saline production conditions and salt management. AGR-04 adds no inherent claim of seawater tolerance or salt balance. AGR-06, “Rapidly programmable, durable crop immunity,” could help manage disease pressures in persistent stands, but immunity alone would not establish competitive repeated harvests, and perenniality does not demonstrate durable immunity.

Roster-based synthesis — AGR-08, “Economically accessible, end-to-end autonomous field farming,” concerns who or what performs farm operations. Perennial crops could change the frequency and type of operations requiring automation, while autonomous systems could manage perennial stands; neither capability establishes the other. AGR-09, “Food crops that reliably build durable, additional soil carbon,” overlaps with possible soil benefits, but requires a distinct demonstration of durable and additional carbon storage. Persistent roots, reduced disturbance or short-term soil-carbon accumulation alone do not complete that concept.

unresolved_issues: The supplied material does not establish the status of a competitive multi-cereal perennial portfolio as of 1 November 2026; no freshness-search results were supplied.
A future demonstration protocol must specify the major-crop portfolio, trial duration, representative environments, competitiveness thresholds and acceptable stand-replacement frequency.
Longer-term productivity, management costs and performance outside the documented irrigated Yunnan settings are not established by the supplied result.
Net environmental benefits require system-specific water-use, soil-carbon and lifecycle emissions assessments, including relevant methane and nitrous oxide effects.
Some PDF pages lack readable extracted content, figure images were uninspected, and supplementary tables were unavailable in the supplied review.
No historical calibration examples were supplied to support a precise comparison with past agricultural breakthroughs.

brief.title: Grain crops that keep yielding after harvest
possible: Farmers could plant major grain crops once and gather competitive harvests for several years as the plants regrow. Across a range of crops and farming conditions, they could maintain grain production while replacing much of the repeated work of establishing a new crop.
why: Repeated planting shapes farmers’ workloads and costs. Crops that regrow could remove recurring jobs such as raising seedlings, ploughing and transplanting. Keeping grain output high while reducing that work could improve farmers’ livelihoods.

sources.showed: They bred perennial rice, which regrows after harvest, and demonstrated repeated harvests with average yields comparable to replanted rice. Farmers also saved labour and input costs.
sources.quote:
These data collectively showed that the PR 
lines we developed had agronomic traits resembling domesticated AR 
yet retained from the perennial O. longistaminata parent the ability to 
regrow vigorously after harvest.
sources.cited_for: Rice demonstrates that regrowth can coexist with repeated, competitive grain production.
sources.not_established: The rice trials do not establish comparable performance across other major grains or all rice-growing conditions.

sources.showed: Kernza, a grain bred from wheatgrass, reduced fertilizer losses into water and changed soil processes compared with annual wheat. Its grain yields remained much lower.
sources.quote:
Carbon mineralization rates beneath kernza during the second year were increased 13% compared 
with annual wheat.
sources.cited_for: A grain crop that regrows can change soil and water conditions before its yields become competitive.
sources.not_established: These results do not demonstrate competitive grain yields or a complete environmental benefit.

shown: Zhang and colleagues demonstrated competitive rice production for four years from one planting in irrigated fields in Yunnan. Average yields per harvest matched replanted rice closely. Pest damage and later yield declines showed that productive regrowth has limits.
missing: Several major grain crops still need to demonstrate competitive, reliable harvests from regrowth across representative farming conditions.
Full farm costs need to include weed and pest control, poor seasons and eventual replacement of the plants.
Complete environmental comparisons need to measure actual water consumption and total emissions, alongside soil changes.

milestones.label: Several grain crops sustain competitive harvests
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to show that several major grains meet preset targets for total yield, survival and reliable regrowth across representative conditions. This would establish the capability beyond rice.

milestones.label: Farmers remain competitive after all costs
milestones.explanation: Farm comparisons would have to count planting savings, ongoing management, failures and eventual crop replacement. This would establish whether repeated harvests offer farmers a workable business.

milestones.label: Complete environmental comparisons establish the balance
milestones.explanation: Comparisons with replanted crops would have to measure soil changes, water use, pests and emissions across production. This would establish whether favourable soil results translate into broader environmental gains.

milestones.label: Independent trials establish where performance holds
milestones.explanation: Independent farming teams would have to reproduce results across sites and seasons, documenting failures and limits. This would establish how reliably the crops perform within tested conditions.

uncertain: Which crops, trial lengths and yield targets should define a successful portfolio, and how often could plants need replacement?
How long can competitive yields last outside the demonstrated irrigated rice settings?
Do soil improvements translate into lower water use and lower total greenhouse-gas emissions, especially in flooded rice?

page.title: Perennial rice, wheat and sorghum at annual-crop yields
page.definition: Rice, wheat and sorghum cultivars regrow after harvest and produce grain for at least three years from one planting. Their cumulative grain yields and net farm returns match or exceed those of replanted annual crops over the same interval within stated production regions.

goal.need: In the Yunnan rice comparison, regrowth saved 68–77 labour days per hectare per harvest cycle. Retaining grain output remains a breeding constraint: a two-year comparison under three management systems found Kernza yields of 4.5% and 33% of annual wheat in successive years. Kernza is intermediate wheatgrass, a separately domesticated perennial cereal.

figures.caption: Perennial rice and annual comparators at three farmer-managed Yunnan sites
rows: Replanted annual rice mean grain yield
Input-cost saving during perennial regrowth cycles
figures.note: Plots covered 1–13 ha. Yield averages describe eight harvests during the first four years after planting in 2016; they are not annual totals or evidence of parity at every site.

completion.title: Perennial rice, wheat and sorghum each match annual crops in three-year grain output and farm returns.
completion.criterion: Rice, wheat and sorghum each have a released cultivar producing grain from the same planting for at least three consecutive years. Field comparisons spanning its stated production region show mean cumulative grain yield per hectare and net farm return at least equal to locally adapted annual comparators over the same interval. Returns include establishment, labour, machinery, inputs, pest control, stand termination and replacement costs, with both grains valued at the comparator's price. The crop set, parity requirements and common-price comparison are Atlas choices.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no external cereal-portfolio completion criterion was found.
completion.basis: Searches of FAO proceedings, NIMSS objectives, breeder goals and domestication roadmaps found no portfolio-wide crop list or yield-and-return pass criterion. This test combines the published three-year definition with breeder goals for grain output and farm viability. Rice, wheat and sorghum delimit the entry; no authoritative definition of the draft's major-grain portfolio was found.

milestones.title: A cereal breeding population combines cultivated ancestry with perennial regrowth.
milestones.criterion: Crosses between an annual cereal and a perennial relative establish breeding material that combines cultivated ancestry with regrowth after harvest. This corresponds to stage II of the published perennial-crop breeding framework. Rice breeding populations produced PR23; the wheat programme reports its first perennial line in 2009; controlled annual–perennial sorghum crosses established breeding populations. The wheat timeline is a developer report, not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: University of Minnesota and collaborating breeders, Kantar and colleagues' four-stage breeding framework, stage II; a published research protocol rather than a regulatory standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: initiating breeding populations by selecting the best genotypes from the available germplasm and making crosses

milestones.title: A perennial cereal produces grain for at least three years without replanting.
milestones.criterion: The same planting supplies grain harvests in at least three consecutive years. Rice PR23 supplied eight consecutive harvests over four years. The wheat programme reports five lines surviving several years, without establishing three annual grain harvests in that account. The cited sorghum paper reports second-season grain yields from rhizome regrowth, which does not establish this three-year test.
milestones.set_by: The Land Institute's Kernza programme, published definition of perennial grains in the Perennial Percent FAQ; applied here across cereals as a developer definition, not certification of these three crops.
milestones.threshold_quote: Perennial grains allow farmers to plant once and harvest a crop for three years or more without replanting.

milestones.title: A perennial cereal cultivar is released for cultivation.
milestones.criterion: Improved breeding material reaches cultivar release, the fourth stage of the published framework. Rice PR23 was released in China in 2018; PR25 and PR107 followed in 2020. Russia's register lists Trititrigia Pamyati Lyubimovoy from 2020 and perennial sorghums Karavan and Travinka from 2004. Those registrations establish release, not three-year grain production or annual-crop yield parity.
milestones.set_by: University of Minnesota and collaborating breeders, Kantar and colleagues' four-stage breeding framework, stage IV; cultivar release is a development stage without a common numerical yield floor.
milestones.threshold_quote: release of cultivars of perennial grain crops

milestones.title: A released perennial cereal matches annual crops in cumulative grain yield over at least three years.
milestones.criterion: A released perennial cereal's mean cumulative grain yield per hectare from one planting over at least three years equals or exceeds locally adapted annual comparators grown over the same interval, in field plots spanning its stated production region. PR23's reported pooled means provide yield parity, with poorer performance at Xinping. The Land Institute reports elite perennial wheat yields at 50–70% of annual cultivars; that undated developer result is not peer reviewed. Corresponding sorghum parity evidence was not found.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of breeder targets, FAO proceedings, NIMSS objectives and published breeding frameworks found no common multiyear yield-parity pass criterion.

not_found: No demonstration satisfying the complete three-cereal yield-and-return test was found.
The supplied Ohio State Kernza PDF returned HTTP 403; the publisher's abstract was accessible.
The opened Russian register establishes cultivar admission but supplies no repeated-harvest grain-yield results.

results.finding: Rice breeding population: lines from F1 through F9 combined cultivated traits with perennial regrowth.
results.detail: The population descended from a cross of cultivated O. sativa and perennial O. longistaminata.
results.quote:
These data collectively showed that the PR 
lines we developed had agronomic traits resembling domesticated AR 
yet retained from the perennial O. longistaminata parent the ability to 
regrow vigorously after harvest.

results.finding: Irrigated perennial rice produced grain for eight harvests over four years from one planting.
results.detail: The four-year result was for PR23 across three locations in southern Yunnan.
results.quote:
From a single 
planting, irrigated perennial rice produced grain for eight consecutive 
harvests over four years, averaging 6.8 Mg ha−1 harvest−1 versus the 6.7 Mg of 
replanted annual rice, which required additional labour and seed.

results.finding: One perennial rice cultivar, PR23, was released to farmers in China in 2018.
results.detail: The paper also reports releases of PR25 and PR107 in China in 2020.
results.quote:
PR23 was released to farmers in China 
in 201835, a key milestone in the commercialization of perennial grains 
bred via interspecific hybridization.

results.finding: PR23 across three locations averaged 6.8 Mg/ha per harvest versus 6.7 for annual rice over eight harvests.
results.detail: The pooled four-year means imply cumulative yield parity. PR23 performed consistently worse than the annual comparator in later seasons at Xinping.
results.quote:
Across the experiment, therefore, PR23 sustain-
ably produced yields averaging 6.8 Mg ha−1 in each of four conse cutive 
years (eight seasons) without re-sowing, and these were comparable to 
yields from the current leading AR cultivars, which averaged 6.7 Mg ha−1 
after being replanted each season (Fig. 2d).

results.finding: Three wheat–Thinopyrum breeding lines exhibited vigorous regrowth after their first harvest.
results.detail: Two lines were derived from common wheat–Thinopyrum hybridization and backcrossed to common wheat. All three regrew in Washington field conditions; waterlogging damaged them in the second year.
results.quote: The perennial lines displayed vigorous regrowth after the initial harvest;

results.finding: Sorghum breeding population: approximately 300 plants survived winter among 400 F2-derived lines from annual–perennial crosses.
results.detail: The crosses used annual cultivated S. bicolor lines and perennial plants derived from S. bicolor–S. halepense populations. Surviving plants were preserved and self-pollinated.
results.quote:
A yield trial
comprising a total of 400 F 2-derived lines in the F 3
from 17 of those annual 9 perennial parental combi-
nations was conducted in the summer of 2005, and
approximately 300 plants that survived through the
following winter were preserved and self-pollinated in
the summer of 2006.

results.finding: Two wheat–wheatgrass derivative entries yielded grain for four consecutive years.
results.detail: The entries were sown in 2008. By years three and four, entries were often represented by only single plants, and grain yields tended to decline as mortality increased.
results.quote: persisted and yielded grain over 4 consecutive years

results.finding: Four perennial wheat–Thinopyrum lines produced grain over three consecutive years from one planting.
results.detail: The field trial in Shanxi, China, began with sowing in October 2011. Grain and forage were harvested each June; grain yield components generally declined as plants aged.
results.quote: Further research is needed to investigate the relationship of grain yields among the 3 years of harvest and develop better adapted perennial wheat that combined the grain yield and perennial habit.

results.finding: Released perennial wheat hybrid Pamyati Lyubimovoy, tested in two sowings, yielded 25.34% less grain than annual wheat.
results.detail: The two crops were sown separately in 2020 and 2021 at one site. Roots died after harvest and no regrowth occurred. The study did not measure cumulative yield from one planting over three years.
results.quote:
Moreover, the combine yield (3.80 tons per 
hectares) falls short compared to the winter wheat variety Stanichnaya (5.09 tons per hectares).
